hdfc_bank_tata_neu_infinity_hdfc_bank.confidence_note:
Every number in this report is ISSUER tier. No aggregator was needed or used - the CardInsider/CardExpert fallback was not opened, and the only aggregator-sourced value in our own data (the Rs 50 redemption fee) is flagged as unsupported rather than confirmed.

Method, for the record: the landing page behaved exactly as the lead predicted - a nav shell with no rates, no fees, no caps. A domain-restricted WebSearch surfaced the official T&C and FAQ PDFs; WebFetch could not read either (both returned 'compressed/encoded PDF stream') but saved them locally, and pdftotext -layout extracted both cleanly. The T&C carries 'Updated on 03-Jan-2026', so this is current documentation, not a stale copy - it even contains changes dated 17-Nov-25 and 26-Dec-25.

On the headline question, are all 15 reward rules real: the brand list is genuine and the cap arithmetic is right, but three rules are not sound. Rule 3 (NeuPass 'bringing total to 10%') states a rate the issuer never publishes and should be removed as a reward_rule. Rule 4 (UPI at 1.5%) is 3x the default rate a user actually gets. Rule 13 (tataneu_bigbasket) double-counts BigBasket. Beyond the rules themselves, the more expensive gaps are structural: four shared category caps split per-brand (Travel inflated 3x), four missing 2,000-NeuCoin category caps on insurance/utility/telecom/grocery, the missing annual fair-usage ceilings, and the missing RuPay-UPI carve-out that silently drops a partner-brand QR payment from 5% to 0.5%.

One genuinely good result worth stating plainly: because 1 NeuCoin = Rs 1 unconditionally, this card carries none of the points-vs-percent unit error that has cost us elsewhere. rp_value_standard = 1.0 is correct, it is the only value the issuer names, and there is no better or worse redemption channel to choose between. The percentages we ship are real percentages.

Two caveats on scope. First, whether our engine actually stacks the two priority-90 tata_neu rules into a displayed 10% is an app-layer question I could not settle from the data file alone - it needs a read of the ranking code before sizing that blast radius. Second, per instructions I made no edits to kredme-data; this is research only. comparison.issuer: 1 EDGE Mile = INR 1 on the Travel EDGE portal (stated twice, in the T&C PDF and on the live product page)
comparison.user_impact: THE HEADLINE GAP. This card's entire value rests on this number and we do not ship it. With rp_value_standard null the engine has no way to convert 2 or 5 EDGE Miles into rupees, so Atlas cannot be ranked honestly against any cashback card. The number is unconditional, plainly stated by the issuer, and free to add.

comparison.issuer: 1 EDGE Mile = 2 Partner Points (Marriott Bonvoy is the exception at 2 EDGE Miles = 1 point)
comparison.user_impact: This is the best redemption channel on the card and we ship nothing for it. A user transferring to an airline partner gets 2 partner points per mile, i.e. double the count they would get spending miles on the Travel EDGE portal. Omitting it makes Atlas look materially worse than it is for exactly the travel-heavy user it is built for.

comparison.field: base_reward_rate / reward_type on the base rule
comparison.issuer: 2 EDGE Miles per INR 100 spent; "EDGE Miles credited cannot be en-cashed."
comparison.user_impact: The 2% magnitude happens to be right at INR 1/mile, but the UNIT is wrong: we type it as cashback. The issuer says in four separate places that EDGE Miles cannot be en-cashed. A user is shown what reads as 2% cash back when in reality they get travel-only miles they must redeem on a portal or transfer to an airline, with a Rs 99 or Rs 199 fee attached. Type is points, not cashback.

comparison.issuer: 5 EDGE Miles per INR 100 spent (i.e. 5% at INR 1/mile), NOT a 5x multiplier
comparison.user_impact: Unit defect. The issuer's 5 is an absolute miles-per-Rs100 rate, not a multiple of the 2-mile base. If the engine reads 5.0 as a multiplier against the 0.02 base it computes 10%, exactly double the true 5%. This is the same points-vs-percent unit error that has bitten us before, and it overstates the card's best category.

comparison.issuer: Travel EDGE portal AND direct airline AND direct hotel spends (airlines MCC 3000-3350 + 4511, hotels MCC 3501-3838 + 7011)
comparison.user_impact: We scope the 5-mile rate to the Axis portal alone. A user booking direct on an airline's own site or paying at a hotel counter earns 5 miles per Rs100 in reality, but our engine will only credit them the 2-mile base. We under-reward the single most common way this card is actually used, and would wrongly recommend a different card for a direct flight booking.

comparison.issuer: "bookings made through any travel agents ... online travel agencies ... shall be eligible for only 2 Miles for every INR 100 spent (base earn)"
comparison.user_impact: The mirror image of the gap above. MakeMyTrip / Cleartrip / Yatra bookings earn only the 2-mile base. If we ever broaden the travel rule to a generic travel category without this carve-out, we will promise 5 miles on OTA spend and be wrong on the highest-value transaction a user makes.

This is a promise the bank has explicitly refused to honour.

Two of the three fuel MCCs are missing. Fuel bought at a merchant coded 5542 (automated fuel dispensers, very common at unmanned pumps) or 5983 will be credited 2 miles per Rs100 by our engine and zero by Axis.

METHOD REPRODUCED. The brief's technique worked exactly as described and needed no aggregator: the sheet's official_url 301-redirects to hdfc.bank.in, that landing page returns a JS navigation shell with zero numbers, and both PDFs then extracted perfectly with `pdftotext -layout` after WebFetch saved them locally. Every fact above is tier "issuer". Zero aggregator numbers were used.

THE LEAD IS CONFIRMED ON EVERY QUOTE HE PULLED. All six of his strings appear verbatim in the T&C PDF: sections 2.2, 2.3 and 2.4; the exclusion list "Fuel, Rent, Government related transactions, EMI, Wallet and Jewellery"; "1 FP = Rs. 0.96"; and "1 Fuel Point = ₹0.2" against statement balance. Nothing he reported is wrong.

FOUR CORRECTIONS/EXTENSIONS TO HIS WORK.
(1) Table 1.1, which he did not extract, is now complete — including the fact he was missing that the 1 FP/Rs 150 tier explicitly says "(including UPI transactions)", and that the grocery and bill-payment caps are 100 FP per month PER CATEGORY, not shared.
(2) The exclusion list he quoted is only the section 2.4 list, scoped to the base tier. A separate, broader section 2.1 lists twelve card-wide no-accrual categories, adding Supermarkets, TAX, Vending Machines, liquor stores, Bakeries, Cash advances and Insurance.
(3) Rs 0.96 is not freely available: it requires manual conversion to XTRAREWARDS, a 500 FP minimum in multiples of 500, and 3-4 working days, and is spendable only as fuel at IOCL pumps.
(4) Rs 0.20 statement credit carries a 12,500 FP minimum and a Rs 50 fee — he reported neither, and the 12,500 minimum is arguably the single most important consumer fact on this card.

UNIT VERIFICATION IS AIRTIGHT. I did not take "5%" on trust. The T&C contains a ten-transaction worked example and I reproduced all four of its arithmetic lines exactly: Rs 3,000 at IOCL = 150 FP, Rs 2,000 grocery = 100 FP, Rs 1,500 electronics = 10 FP, Rs 5,250 UPI = 35 FP. So "5%" means the POINT COUNT equals 5% of the rupees spent — 1 FP per Rs 20 — and the rupee value is that count times the point value. True value on IOCL fuel is 4.8% only via IOCL free fuel, and 1.0% on the unconditional channels. We ship it as reward_type "cashback_pct" at 0.05, which reads as 5% cash. That 5x overstatement is the most consequential finding here and it is the same class of unit error the memory flags as our most expensive recurring defect.

TWO ITEMS I DELIBERATELY DID NOT RESOLVE, rather than guess. The fuel-surcharge Rs 400-5,000 range is marked UNVERIFIABLE because the only sentence stating it enumerates six other HDFC cards and omits Indian Oil — our shipped values may well be right, but the document does not say so. The 3.50% forex markup is marked AGREES with a caveat because it comes from a merged column cell spanning a page break; no competing value appears between it and the Indian Oil row, but it is a layout inference, not a labelled cell.

ONE ISSUER SELF-CONTRADICTION worth escalating before any publish: Table 1.1 pays 5% on Grocery MCC 5411, while section 2.1 item 4 says no points accrue on "Supermarkets". Both sentences are in the same PDF. I would not raise the grocery rule's confidence above medium until that is resolved with the bank.

FINALLY, a scope note: the two PDFs are dated Mar-2025 (fees, "Version 2.5") and the T&C references changes through 1 August 2024. Today is 20 August 2026, so both are the current published documents but neither is recent. Given the memory note that HDFC moved Rs 150 to Rs 200 on other cards in May, it is worth confirming this card's Rs 150 threshold has not moved before treating these rates as current-dated. axis_bank_flipkart_axis_bank_super_elite.confidence_note:
High confidence on the earn structure, the caps and the whole fee table - all of it came from the issuer's own domain, most of it twice over. The technique in the brief worked exactly as described: WebFetch on the landing page returned a navigation shell and nothing else, the card's own T&C PDF extracted perfectly with pdftotext -layout, and the browser then rendered the same page into a complete earn table and fee table. Three independent Axis surfaces (product page FAQ, 'Special features' panel, T&C PDF) agree on 12 / 6 / 2 SuperCoins per Rs 100, so the earn rates are settled.

The card is NOT withdrawn. I checked this specifically because the brief flagged it: it is listed in the live 62-page MITC fee table, its T&C PDF is current, its product page renders in full with a forward-looking 28-Aug-2026 revision banner, and Flipkart's own Super Elite store page was crawled 11-Aug-2026. The retirement signal circulating in search results is a misattribution - the 20-June-2025 revision that kills four lounge visits and cuts the welcome voucher applies to the base cashback Flipkart Axis Bank Credit Card. Both documents share almost the same title, which is how they get confused. One caveat I could not close: this card has no Apply Now button while its page-mates do, which is consistent with being closed to new applications but live for existing holders. I could not evidence that either way, so I have not claimed it.

Two things are genuinely unverifiable and I have not papered over them. First, the fuel surcharge waiver: the issuer advertises the benefit and publishes no numbers for this card, and the MITC lists dozens of Axis cards by name in its fuel clause without listing this one. Our shipped Rs 5,000 ceiling and Rs 400 monthly cap are unsourced; the MITC's most common band is Rs 400 to Rs 4,000. Second, the SuperCoin rupee value: Flipkart states outright that SuperCoins carry no assigned monetary value, so our rp_value_standard of 1.0 is not a slightly-wrong number but a number with no issuer basis at all, sitting at the optimistic end of the 0.75-1.0 range aggregators use. Since that field drives ranking and not only display, it inflates this card against properly-verified competitors.

On units, which the brief rightly called the expensive error: every rate on this card is in POINTS, not percent. CardInsider renders them as '12% / 6% / 2% SuperCoins', which is exactly the trap. Twelve coins per Rs 100 is 12% in coins; at 0.75-1.0 per coin the real return is 9-12%.

The most consequential finding for users is not any of the above - it is that base_reward_rate ships as 0.0 while the issuer states 2 SuperCoins per Rs 100 on all eligible spends, uncapped, in three separate places. That fake zero base drops the card to last place in every non-Flipkart ranking. Close behind it: rent is flagged as counting toward the Rs 2 lakh fee waiver when Axis explicitly excludes it, so a rent-paying user will believe they have earned a waiver and still be charged Rs 500. Neither of those needs an app release; both are data fixes. I made no edits to kredme-data, per the brief.

axis_bank_indianoil_axis_bank_premium.confidence_note:
HIGH CONFIDENCE. Every fact above is tier "issuer" - no aggregator was used, and the step-4 fallback was not needed. Four Axis Bank PDFs carried the whole result, all extracted locally with pdftotext -layout: the Premium card's own member T&C, its 20-Jun-2025 revision notice, the bank-wide Schedule of Fees and Charges, and the EDGE REWARDS master T&C. As the brief predicted, both HTML landing pages returned nothing but a navigation shell, the value-chart URL 301'd away and the fees-and-charges URL 404'd; the PDFs extracted perfectly.

Three things give this unusual strength. First, the two most load-bearing numbers are each confirmed by two independent issuer documents: the INR 30,000 fee waiver appears in the card T&C clause 3.2 and again in the Schedule of Charges, and the 1 EDGE Mile = INR 1 value appears in the card T&C clause 5.1 and again in the EDGE REWARDS cashback table that names "IndianOil Axis Bank Premium Credit Card" in a row of its own. Second, the T&C contains a worked illustrative example that resolves the clause-5.3 ambiguity about whether the 600-Mile fuel cap is a total or accelerated-only - it is a TOTAL (100 base + 500 accelerated on INR 15,000), and the same example proves the grocery 33 is accelerated-ONLY (33 + 33 = 66 on INR 5,000). Those two caps are therefore expressed in different units despite looking parallel, which is precisely the trap our data fell into. Third, the Schedule of Charges fee table was verified by measuring character offsets rather than eyeballing columns, and the resulting product-to-fee mapping independently reproduces eleven known Axis card fees (Samsung Infinite 5,000; Vistara Infinite 10,000; SuperMoney RuPay 0; etc.), so the INDIAN OIL Premium column assignment is sound.

On units, which the brief rightly called the expensive error: this is a pure EDGE Miles card - the Premium T&C uses "EDGE Mile" 56 times and "EDGE REWARD Point" zero times. Axis runs two currencies at a 5x difference (EDGE REWARD Points at INR 0.20, EDGE Miles at INR 1.00), and the same EDGE REWARDS table shows both side by side. Our shipped rp_value_standard of 1.0 is CORRECT. The real exposure is the opposite of the usual one: someone applying the familiar "Axis points are worth INR 0.20" heuristic would cut every reward figure on this card by 80%. Labelling reward_currency as generic "reward_points" instead of EDGE Miles is what leaves that door open.

Biggest finding by user impact is not any single wrong number but base_reward_rate = 0.0. Both reward rules are multipliers (6.0 and 2.0) resting on a zero base, so the engine currently computes zero reward for this card on fuel, on groceries and everywhere else, when the true rates are 4.0%, 1.333% and 0.667%. The card ranks last in exactly the comparison it should win. Second is the fee waiver at 3.3x reality (100,000 shipped vs 30,000 actual). Third is the fuel surcharge block, where 400/5000/400 are Axis's generic terms rather than this product's uncapped ones.

Two honest limitations. The Travel Edge 0.25 comes from the EDGE REWARDS SMS-based redemption grid, which names our card's column explicitly but describes a mechanism that may not be identical to redeeming against a Travel Edge booking; the card's own T&C states no rate for that row. I have reported 0.25 with that caveat rather than presenting it as settled. And the IOCL XtraRewards channel is genuinely unresolvable from issuer sources - only a 3:10 ratio into a currency Axis never prices - so our shipped 1.0 at confidence "medium" is unsupported and I have marked it UNVERIFIABLE rather than substituting a guess. No file in kredme-data was modified; this was research only.

kotak_mahindra_bank_indianoil_kotak.confidence_note:
HIGH CONFIDENCE, ISSUER-TIER THROUGHOUT. No aggregator was used or needed — the CardInsider/CardExpert/Finology fallback was never reached, so every number above comes from kotak.bank.in or a PDF on that domain.

METHOD NOTE THAT MATTERS FOR THE OTHER NINE CARDS: the landing page rendered fine here (not the expected JS shell), but it only carries marketing percentages. The real data was in two PDFs that WebFetch's summarizer explicitly refused, calling them "heavily compressed" and recommending I contact customer service. Both extracted perfectly with `pdftotext -layout`. Treat a WebFetch PDF refusal as "run pdftotext", never as "unavailable" — the MITC alone answered nine fields the HTML pages could not.

THE CENTRAL FINDING, STATED PLAINLY: every percentage Kotak advertises on this card — 4%, 2%, 0.5% — is computed at Rs 0.25 per point, the MERCHANDISE catalogue rate. The MITC proves this against itself: it glosses "1200 Reward Points" as "(Rs 300)" and "800 Reward Points" as "(Rs 200)", and 300/1200 = 250/1000 = exactly Rs 0.25. The only unconditional cash channel pays Rs 0.20. So the honest cash rates are fuel 3.20%, grocery/dining 1.60%, everything else 0.40% — uniformly 80% of the advertised figure. Our rp_value_standard=0.2 is already right; the rates just have to be read through it.

THE COMPLAINT REPRODUCES, AND THE DATA IS NOT AT FAULT. The user saw 12% because our dining/grocery rule stores reward_rate=12.0 meaning "12 points per Rs 150", and a display surface printed that number with a percent sign. The stored value and its unit are both correct in cards.json. The fuel rule has the identical defect and is worse in magnitude: 24 renders as 24% against a true 3.20%. This is a rendering fix plus a publish, not a data edit — consistent with the earlier read on this card.

WHAT I WOULD TREAT AS MORE URGENT THAN THE DISPLAY BUG: the missing UPI rule. This is a RuPay card built for scanning a QR at a fuel pump, and Kotak pays only 0.5% on any UPI transaction across every category. We have no channel='upi' rule at all, so we promise 24 points per Rs 150 on precisely the payment method the card is marketed for, where the user actually receives 3 — and loses the fuel surcharge waiver as well. That is a benefit that does not exist, not merely a number shown wrong.

THREE THINGS I DELIBERATELY DID NOT RESOLVE. (1) The welcome-benefit trigger is contradicted between Kotak's own MITC and its own marketing page; I reported both rather than picking one, and it should not be presented as certain either way. (2) Whether the 24-point fuel rate is restricted to MID/TID-identified IndianOil outlets the way the surcharge waiver explicitly is — the MITC is silent, so I left it open rather than inferring from the adjacent sentence. (3) No minimum transaction value for earning exists in any issuer document; our nulls are correct by evidence, not by default.

One caution for whoever acts on this: do not "correct" rp_value_standard from 0.20 to 0.25 to make our percentages match Kotak's marketing. That would inflate every rate on this card by 25% and would be the same class of error as the one that produced this complaint."

HIGH confidence. Every number above came from HDFC Bank's own domain - no aggregator was needed or used, so nothing here is tagged aggregator tier.

Method, since it worked cleanly and is worth reusing: WebFetch on both PDFs returned unusable binary and the model in the loop said it could not read them - but it saved them locally and named the path. pdftotext -layout on those saved files gave the complete document, including the Annex 1 Fair Usage table that is the single most valuable thing on this card. The two JS-rendered HTML pages (landing, value-chart) returned navigation shells to WebFetch exactly as warned; the browser read them fine. One extra trick worth recording: the AMP mirror at v.hdfc.bank.in/amp/... IS static and extracted the headline rates via plain WebFetch before I opened the browser. The value-chart path exists but is JS-rendered and added nothing the landing page did not already give.

One number I deliberately did not take from the obvious place: the MITC fees PDF appears to state a 3.5% foreign currency fee, but I checked the word bounding boxes with pdftotext -bbox and confirmed there is NO text at that column's x-coordinate on the Tata Neu Plus page - the 3.50% visible elsewhere belongs to a different merged cell group. The 3.5% in my facts comes from the issuer's own fees-and-charges page instead, where it is stated for this card by name.

Where the shipped data is right, it is right for the right reason: the six 2% brand caps are exact rupee-to-NeuCoin conversions of Annex 1 (Rs 3,00,000 x 2% = 6,000), so whoever entered them understood the unit. The defect is structural, not arithmetic - the issuer shares one cap across a brand GROUP and we split it per brand, which inflates the Stay group's real ceiling threefold.

Two things I want to flag as the real risk on this card, both of which would show a user a number they will not receive. First, the UPI rule: we ship a flat 1% when the default is 0.25% and the other 0.75% requires the Tata Neu UPI ID and lands in a different account - a 4x overstatement on the most common everyday payment method, with a 500 NeuCoin/month cap we do not carry. Second, the 7% Tata Neu rule: the issuer never writes 7% anywhere. It is 2% from the card plus a 5% NeuPass programme benefit that requires separate registration, is limited to unspecified 'selected categories', and explicitly excludes Air India, Tanishq, Cult.fit, Tata Play and Tata Pay bill payments. Every rule on this card currently carries confidence 'low', which is at least honest - but the app defaults a missing confidence to 'high', so it is worth checking how these render.

Finally, a staleness signal: the lounge benefit stopped being unconditional on 10-Jun-2025 and is now a Rs 50,000-per-quarter milestone, and the MCC 5816 gaming exclusion dates from 1-Jul-2025. Neither reached our data. The T&C PDF I read is stamped 03-Jan-2026 and the FAQ 07-Jan-2026, so both are current as of today.

HIGH CONFIDENCE on every number reported. This card went unusually well: zero aggregator fallback was needed. The issuer publishes a 25-page 'Product Feature Document' at https://www.idfcfirst.bank.in/content/dam/idfcfirstbank/pdf/Hello-Cashback-Terms-and-Conditions.pdf that extracts perfectly with pdftotext -layout (1,111 lines) and contains the complete cashback table, both caps, the exclusion list, an MCC map for every essential category, and seven worked illustrations that let me verify the cap arithmetic against the bank's own maths rather than infer it. The MITC gave the fee and forex rows; the browser gave the FD terms after WebFetch returned the expected navigation shell.

METHOD NOTE confirming the brief: WebFetch on the landing page returned exactly 'This page is only a navigation shell with no card details' - the predicted dead end. The T&C PDF found via domain-restricted WebSearch was the unlock, as it was for IndianOil HDFC. Two of the three PDFs I pulled needed local pdftotext because WebFetch could only see the binary. One issuer PDF (the Product Guide) is image-only and yielded nothing; it did not matter.

ANSWER TO THE HEADLINE QUESTION: This is a genuine cashback card, not points dressed as cashback. The T&C defines it unambiguously - '1 Cashback = Rs 1' - credited straight to the card account, with no catalogue, no tiers and no alternate redemption channel. Our rp_value_standard of 1.0 is correct and unconditional. This card should be marked as verified-safe against any future point-value or unit sweep.

WHERE THE REAL DAMAGE IS, ranked. (1) We pay 1% on FUEL, which the issuer names in its exclusion sentence - a fabricated rule on a category that earns zero, made more confusing by the real 1% fuel-surcharge waiver sitting next to it. (2) The Rs 1,500 overall per-cycle cap is entirely absent, and our 1% essential rules are uncapped, so high rent/jewellery spend shows unbounded cashback. (3) The Rs 1,000 online cap is duplicated across the 3% and 5% rules instead of shared, overstating online headroom by up to 2x. (4) exclusion_rules is an empty array against four published exclusion classes - most damagingly third-party UPI, which is the natural behaviour for a card that links to GPay and PhonePe. (5) has_rupay_upi is 0 on a card the issuer lists under 'UPI Credit Cards'. (6) The FD-backed nature is invisible: no user is told they must lock up Rs 10,000.

TWO THINGS I WOULD FLAG BEYOND THE FIELD LIST. First, the MAD condition - miss one minimum payment and the entire cycle's cashback is forfeited, not reduced - is the single most consequential fact on this card and appears nowhere in our record, on a product the issuer explicitly sells to people with no credit score. Second, our confidence stamps are inverted here: thirteen rules that are true and now issuer-verifiable all sit at 'low', carrying the exact same stamp as the one fuel rule that is false. On this card the confidence field distinguishes nothing.

THREE CAVEATS ON WHAT I AM CALLING ISSUER-VERIFIED. First, the forex markup: 3.50% sits in a merged cell in the MITC fee table, printed once on page 3, with the Foreign Currency column blank for every row below including MoneyBack's on page 4. I verified with pdftotext -bbox that no competing value exists in that column for MoneyBack's row, so the reading is sound, but it is a structural inference from a table rather than a sentence naming the card. Second, the grocery cap of 1,000 points/month and the insurance cap of 2,000/day both rest on 'the rest of the cards' / 'all other credit cards' catch-alls after a named premium list that excludes MoneyBack - correct, but by exclusion. Third, the milestone T&C PDF is genuinely unreachable, so the milestone amounts are verified but the exclusions that apply to milestone-qualifying spend are not.

THE UNIT POINT, because it is where this card gets misread. Every earn rate on the MoneyBack is in POINTS, never percent. '4 Reward Points per Rs 150 online' is not 4%, and it is not even 2.67% - at the unconditional Rs 0.20 statement value it is 0.53%. The base rate is 0.18%. This is a genuinely weak card and our data should say so; the danger is someone converting '2X Reward Points' into a percentage and shipping a rate roughly fifteen times the truth. The Rs 99 redemption fee makes it worse still: on a minimum 2,500-point redemption worth Rs 500, the fee alone takes about 23%, so the realistic floor value of a point here is nearer Rs 0.155 than Rs 0.20.

BIGGEST USER-FACING DEFECTS, in order. (1) base_reward_rate = 0.0 when the issuer clearly states 2 RP per Rs 150 - this makes the card rank last on every offline swipe and also breaks the online rule, because past the 500-point cap HDFC drops the user to 2 RP per Rs 150 while our engine drops them to zero.
